51.4: The Patriarchs Established Them And the Sages Based Them On Sacrifices. This means that certainly the patriarchs established [prayer], but from this establishment alone we would not have been obligated to say [the prayers]. So the sages came and based them on sacrifices so that we would be obligated.

52.5: And he did not interrupt the prayer of Rabbi Yirmiyah, as he did not step in front of him - And we learn from this that it is forbidden to pass in front of people praying, and specifically in front of their faces, but regarding their sides we aren't worried about just passing by.

75.0: And the halakha follows the Sages regarding ha-motzi ("who brings forth"). This is why it was necessary to rule according to the Sages, because regarding motzi ("brings forth"), everyone agrees and does not dispute. Nevertheless, ha-motzi is preferable in this case because it can imply past, present, and future. Additionally, wheat is one of the types of grains that constantly sprout, unlike the fruits of trees, which only bear fruit at specific times. Therefore, it is fitting to bless over them with borei ("who creates") rather than ha-borei ("the one who creates"), as they do not grow continuously. And since the Sages established the blessing borei for the fruit of trees, they similarly established borei for produce of the ground as well, to maintain consistency in blessings over fruits. However, in the Jerusalem Talmud, it is stated that the reasoning of the Sages regarding ha-motzi is to avoid merging consecutive letters, meaning that one should not say melekh ha-olam motzi ("King of the world, who brings forth"), in order to create a separation between connected words. Some say that the halakha allows even motzi, and thus one may recite motzi as well. However, the correct explanation is the first one, and this is the common practice.

85.1: Ces sigli (סיגלי) – ce sont des herbes tendres qui ont une odeur corporelle – on récite sur elles la bénédiction « qui crée des herbes odoriférantes » (boré isbé besamim). Le narkom de ginonita – ce sont des herbes odorantes mais dures – on récite sur elles la bénédiction « qui crée des arbres odoriférants » (boré atsé besamim). Le d’davra – qui est tendre – on récite dessus boré isbé besamim. Mais pour les fleurs, qu’elles poussent sur un arbre ou sur une herbe, dans tous les cas, on récite sur leur parfum la bénédiction « Béni soit Celui qui a donné une bonne odeur aux fruits » (Baroukh shenatan reach tov baferot), comme nous l’avons écrit plus haut :
85.2: Celui qui sent un étrog ou une pomme de coing récite : Baroukh shenatan reach tov baferot. C’est-à-dire : bien que leur usage principal soit pour la consommation et qu’ils ne soient pas faits pour le parfum, puisque l’on a l’intention de les sentir, on récite la bénédiction. Mais si l’on n’a pas l’intention de sentir, même si on perçoit et profite de l’odeur, on ne récite pas de bénédiction – sauf dans le cas d’une chose faite spécifiquement pour le parfum, comme cela sera démontré plus loin.
